items.name: The sea in late October and November
items.teaser: Expect roughly 17–20C in November, falling through the month; early November has often read 18–21C
items.story: The honest range for Dubrovnik's sea in November is about 17 to 20C, and the sources disagree because they use different data. Seatemperature.net gives a November average of 20C, with a 16C low and a 22C high, and its daily tables for 2022 to 2025 show mostly 18 to 21C in early November. Holiday-weather puts the month at 17C, Beach-weather at 18C and calls it too cold for long swims. The water cools week by week, so late October is still the better end. A hard bura or a long jugo can change it in a day.
items.why: Swim from the rocks at midday on a calm, sunny day, and give anyone who feels the cold a wetsuit.
facts: Late Oct to end Nov, cooling week by week

items.name: Lokrum and the island boats in winter
items.teaser: Jadrolinija's off-season timetable began on 28 September; Lokrum's boats thin out and may stop
items.story: The islands slow down rather than close. Jadrolinija's 2026 timetables split the year: the off-season runs from 1 January to 28 May and from 28 September to 31 December, so the Elaphiti line from Gruž and the Sobra–Prapratno car ferry to Mljet are already on their winter times. Mljet is a summer day trip: in winter the catamaran's hours do not allow a same-day return to Dubrovnik. Lokrum's boats from the Old Port run less often after the summer; the reserve's own notice for 2025 had the island reopening on 1 February with weekend boats only until 1 April, and no 2026 winter notice was found.

items.name: The city walls on winter hours
items.teaser: From 1 November the walls are listed as open 9:00 to 15:00, with last entry about half an hour before
items.story: The full circuit of the walls is about 1,940 metres, and in summer the warning is heat; in November it is the clock. Several ticket and travel sites list winter hours from 1 November of 9:00 to 15:00, through to March, with last entry about 30 minutes before closing. The official site could not be checked, and prices are argued: most sources give 40 EUR for adults and 15 EUR for children aged 7 to 18, others 35 EUR, and one a winter rate of 20 EUR from November to February that no other source repeats. The low sun lights the Bokar and Minčeta stone in the early afternoon.
items.why: Start by 13:00 at the latest: the loop takes about an hour and a half, and the gates close at 15:00.
facts: Adult 40 EUR in most listings (35 EUR or a 20 EUR winter rate in others); child 15 EUR

items.story: An hour up the coast, the walls of Ston climb the hill between Ston and Mali Ston, built by the Republic to guard the salt pans below. items.name: The mandarin harvest in the Neretva delta
items.teaser: Late September to mid-November: the only place, they say, where mandarins are harvested by boat
items.story: An hour and a half north of Dubrovnik, around Opuzen, the Neretva delta is Croatia's mandarin country, averaging about 43,000 tonnes a year between 2010 and 2024 according to a Croatian agricultural paper. Visit Dubrovnik gives the harvest as late September to mid-November, with October and November the peak. Some plantations sit on islands between the channels and are reached only by the lađa, the flat wooden boat of the delta. Agencies sell days that combine a boat ride, picking with a basket to take home and a tasting, often with brudet, fried eels and mandarin liqueur. This year's early fruit is reported smaller after a dry, hot summer.
items.why: Go before mid-November, and buy a crate from the roadside stalls on the way home.
facts: Late Sep–mid Nov; peak Oct and Nov

items.name: Clocks back and the November holidays
items.teaser: Clocks go back on Sunday 25 October; All Saints on 1 November and Remembrance Day on 18 November are holidays
items.story: Three dates change the shape of the weeks ahead. On Sunday 25 October the clocks go back an hour, as across the EU, and sunset jumps to late afternoon. Wednesday 18 November is Remembrance Day, the public holiday for the victims of the war and of Vukovar, and shops and offices close. items.name: Festa sv. Vlaha, St Blaise Day, 3 February
items.teaser: The city's feast since the 10th century, UNESCO-listed in 2009; šporki makaruli in restaurants all week
items.story: St Blaise has been Dubrovnik's patron since the city's tradition places his apparition in 972, warning of a Venetian attack. UNESCO inscribed the festivity in 2009. On 3 February the relics are carried in procession down Stradun, and the Rector, now a ceremonial role, leads the city. Around it the tourist board runs the Days of Šporki Makaruli: in 2026, from 31 January to 4 February, 19 restaurants served the dark beef ragù on thick pasta. A tombola in front of the Sponza Palace at 16:00 on the feast day, tickets 2 EUR, is part of it. In 2027 the feast falls on a Wednesday.
items.why: Book the week, not the day: the šporki menus run five days around the feast.

items.name: Holy Week and Easter in Konavle
items.teaser: Woven palms on Palm Sunday, wax-patterned eggs on Holy Saturday; Easter 2027 falls on 28 March
items.story: Easter in Konavle is a family feast with its own small customs. On Palm Sunday the faithful carry woven palm fronds and olive branches in procession; the palm weaving came to Konavle only about sixty years ago, and before that people carried a bundle called the Blessing for a year's health. Women dye eggs on Good Friday or Holy Saturday, laying patterns in wax and colouring them with onion skins, and families in mourning keep plain boiled eggs. Easter Sunday 2027 is 28 March, Palm Sunday 21 March. The Čilipi Sunday folklore season opens at Easter.
items.why: Go to Mass in a Konavle village on Palm Sunday, then stay for the Čilipi folklore the following Sunday.

items.story: The festival opened in 1950 and keeps the same dates every year, 10 July to 25 August. The 77th edition in 2026 ran 47 days with more than 70 performances and over 2,000 artists, among them Joshua Bell with the Academy of St Martin in the Fields on 14 July. It opens at night in front of St Blaise's Church with the Libertas flag raised. Its stages are the city itself: the Rector's Palace atrium, Fort Revelin and Lovrijenac, the fort above the sea where Marko Fotez set Hamlet in the early 1950s, a production the festival has returned to many times. The 78th edition's programme is not yet published.

items.name: The salt harvest at Ston, late July to September
items.teaser: The salt is raked by hand in the hottest dry weeks of late summer, and rain can delay it
items.story: Ston's summer is the salt harvest. When the sun has done its work in the crystallization pools, the salt is gathered quickly by hand over a few dry days, most years between late July and September. Weather sets the date: one report from Lider describes a year when rain at the end of July delayed the start, then 55 tonnes came out of the St Francis pool on the first day. The salt works take summer volunteers for the harvest, and a stand at the gate usually sells bags of salt in season. No 2026 harvest report was found.
items.why: Visit in the early morning, when the rakers work before the heat.

bougie.title: 1333 — the salt of Ston and its guarding walls
bougie.desc: Why the Republic bought a peninsula, walled a hillside and lived on the white crust of a few shallow pools.
bougie.lede: In 1333 Dubrovnik took Ston and the Pelješac peninsula, and what it wanted was the salt. The shallow pans at the head of the Ston channel became the Republic's most profitable export, and the walls that still climb the hill above them were built to keep that salt in Ragusan hands for nearly five centuries.
paras: Salt was made at Ston long before Ragusa: one source mentions the settlement with salt in 167 BC, and others trace the working back to Roman times. What changed in 1333 was ownership, when Dubrovnik acquired Ston and Pelješac, bought from the local lords in the tourism accounts; some guides say 1334. UNESCO's tentative-list entry calls salt the Republic's most important and most profitable export, and ties the layout of the pans to the town's planning.

The walls cross the narrowest neck of the peninsula from Ston to Mali Ston: more than 7 km at first, about 5.5 km today. Their start is argued: one source gives building from 1333 to 1506, Wikipedia gives 1358, after the Pelješac purchase. How much the salt earned is argued too. Tourism sources repeat that it brought about a third of the Republic's income, and one gives 15,900 ducats a year, but no scholarly source for either figure was found.

The pans are still worked. Solana Ston has 58 pools in five groups, nine of them for crystallization, and makes about 500 tonnes of salt a year. The harvest is done by hand in the dry weeks of late summer, mostly late July to September, and rain can push it back, as late-July rain did in one reported year. No 2026 harvest report was found.
